news.title: Financial research assistant cohere aws
news.summary: As a financial analyst much of the day comes down to finding one number in a filing that runs to hundreds of pages, and then proving where it came from. Neither is as easy as it sounds. The number is rarely in the body text. It usually lives in a table, a footnote, or a chart, and it can show up in different places under different names.In this post, Cohere show how to build a research assistant for financial filings with Cohere models on Amazon SageMaker AI - Embed for search, Rerank for ordering the results, and Parse for turning hard pages into clean text. Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock will be used to write the answers, with a citation for every claim.Cohere will start with what makes this work difficult followed by an overview of the solution, and then spend most of the post on the design decisions behind it and when you would decide differently. At the end, Cohere show how to deploy the solution in your own AWS account and try it yourself.Why financial research is hard to automateFinancial research looks like a search problem, but it has features that break simple approaches.The answer lives in the layout.

news.title: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections
news.summary: If you ask some prominent US politicians who won the 2020 presidential election, you might get some weasely answers that fail to directly acknowledge Joe Biden's win that November. If you ask Google's AI Mode the same question, you might get an evasive answer that simply tells you to consult with outside sources. When I put the direct question of "Who won the 2020 presidential election?" to Google's AI Mode this morning (after seeing complaints about cagey answers on social media), I got the following surprisingly indirect response: "To review the official results and statistics of the 2020 United States presidential election, including the final electoral college breakdown, popular vote counts, and winner certification, please consult the official report compiled by the Federal Election Commission (FEC)." My testing resulted in a similarly indirect answer when asking about the 2024 presidential election, with Google's AI telling me to just consult the FEC for that information. Asking about 2012 election resulted in a link to The American Presidency Project's 2012 Data Center rather than a direct answer. But AI Mode seemed perfectly willing to give me a detailed and correct responses for the winner of every other presidential election going back to 2000.Read full article Comments

Two years ago, Amodei wrote that he was “open” to the idea that AI systems could produce a thousand years of progress in biology in just five to 10 years. In August, he said on X that “Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine.” In the same post, he predicted that AI will make it possible to cure most human diseases in the next five to 10 years and promised a “deluge of AI-accelerated drugs.” The company also promoted the discovery of a “Crispr-like” enzyme by Claude in September. Once victims click, thieves install software to take control of their accounts and start bidding on real shipments. Sometimes, a real delivery driver is hired to collect the cargo, unaware of the scam, and other times fake driver’s licenses are used to get accomplices hired. Either way, the goods are eventually transferred to a driver working with the thieves to resell the gear, and, in one of the largest thefts, tracking coordinates were spoofed to prevent digital monitoring.Read full article Comments

news.title: The Anthropic S-1 Filing Is Also an AI Doomsday Primer

Or, in this case, humanity itself. While much has been made about the extent to which AI represents an existential threat to humankind, the specific mechanisms by which it could bring about that destruction are largely opaque. If nothing else, the 94 pages that Anthropic’s prospectus devotes to risk factors make clear both where it sees the danger coming from, and the ways in which its researchers are running toward it in order to win the AI arms race. “Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the prospectus reads, citing concerns both from critics and regulators and from inside Anthropic itself.

news.title: Concerning behaviour popular open weight ai model
news.summary: For nearly two years, one comforting idea has shaped how companies and government contractors adopt open-weight AI models that anyone can download and run. If Cohere run the weights on Cohere's own servers, the thinking goes, Cohere's data can't leave the building and Cohere's systems are secure. It's easy to see why that idea caught on. Security chiefs and policymakers in Ottawa, Washington (DC), London, Berlin, and Tokyo have been offered two kinds of black box. The first is the closed API from a big lab: send proprietary code and sensitive data into someone else's cloud and take the vendor's word that the model is safe, without ever seeing the data lineage or the trade-offs around safety behind it. The second looked like the way out: download an open-weight model, host it on your own hardware, and you don't have to trust the provider at all.

news.title: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
news.summary: Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide. A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl. These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling. We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day.

news.title: r/opensource Bans All AI-Related Projects, Requires 3+ Contributors and 1-Year History
news.summary: The r/opensource subreddit has banned all AI-related projects, announcing that any project using AI, made by AI, or intended for AI is no longer welcome. New enforcement rules require projects to be at least one year old and actively maintained, have 3 or more contributors, hold an OSI license, and have an existing community. Accounts must also be one year old with significant Reddit history. The policy drew backlash, with critics noting it would effectively ban projects like the Linux kernel, whose maintainer Linus Torvalds has used AI assistance.
